title: Cranial imaging window implantation technique for longitudinal multimodal imaging of the brain environment in live mice
protocol: Shave the mouse's scalp.
Make an incision into the shaved and clean scalp.
Etch the skull mechanically.
Etch the skull chemically.
Anesthetize the mouse with isoflurane inhalation anesthesia (3.5% isoflurane/O2 for induction, and 2% isoflurane/O2 for maintenance).
Pinch the mouse's toes with surgical tweezers to assess full anesthesia.
Place the mouse on a heating pad covered by a liquid-absorbable bed mat.
Ensure continuous isoflurane inhalation anesthesia through a nose mask.
Prevent contact with cold surfaces to maintain normal body temperature during anesthesia.
Shave the fur on the top of the scalp.
Apply eye ointment.
Clean the shaved scalp with ethanol and betadine pads sequentially, repeating this procedure three times.
Apply eye ointment again.
Inject 50 μL of a mixture containing 4.4 mg/mL lidocaine and 2.8 mg/mL bupivacaine subcutaneously under the scalp.
Inject 100 μL of 0.02 mg/mL buprenorphine subcutaneously in the upper back of the mouse.
After 2 minutes, allow the lidocaine/bupivacaine mixture to take effect.
Use a scalpel to make an incision into the skin overlaying the scalp, cutting longitudinally between the eyes as far as the back of the skull.
Keep the scalpel blade flat and cut very gently to avoid damaging blood vessels in the skull underneath.
If bleeding occurs, place a piece of Gelfoam on the damaged site while gently applying pressure until the bleeding stops.
Dry the skull.
Remove the periosteum with a cotton swab.
Mechanically etch the skull with a scalpel by making a pattern of crosses on the bone.
Mechanically etch the skull, avoiding major blood vessels.
Wipe the skull once with a cotton swab moistened in 35% phosphoric acid.
Clean the skull with a cotton swab again to assess proper etching.
Move the mouse onto the stereotactic apparatus and restrain the head in an EPE foam mold.
Apply new eye ointment if necessary.
Use a disposable Pasteur pipette to moisten and clean the exposed skull.
Place the mouse on the stereotaxic frame.
Rinse the skull extensively with Ringer’s solution to remove excess 35% phosphoric acid.
Remove a part of the scalp, while leaving sufficient skin around the eyes.
Place sliding lock forceps on the side of the planned craniotomy to gain better access to the surgical area.
Perform craniotomy using the 3-mm biopsy punch and carefully remove the bone flap.
Optional: Induce glioblastoma formation by injecting RCAS virus-producing DF-1 cells into Tva transgenic mice using a Hamilton syringe.
Place the CIW (left image) and put Loctite super glue on the edge of the 5-mm coverslip while gently pressing the CIW with a blunt forceps.
Glue head bar next to the implanted CIW using Loctite super glue.
Apply dental cement to the exposed skull and wait until it solidifies before removing the mouse from the surgery table.
Use surgical scissors to remove part of the scalp, approximately 4 mm frontally and caudally, and 2 mm laterally on each side.
Use forceps with a sliding lock to grasp the skin on the side of the craniotomy to have better access to the surgical site.
Use a sterile cotton swab to remove the periosteum and dry the area of the craniotomy located in the skull overlaying the right frontal cortex.
Place a 3-mm biopsy punch on the skull and slowly turn it in both directions to etch the bone.
Continue until the round bone flap becomes loose and almost detaches from the skull, then carefully remove it with forceps.
Perform a craniotomy using a biopsy punch.
Ensure there is ample space between the craniotomy site and major blood vessels, including the sagittal suture and bregma.
Slowly turn the biopsy punch while applying minimal pressure to maintain precision.
Regularly check if the bone flap starts to detach by gently pressing with forceps.
If the bone flap detaches when minimal pressure is applied, adjust the position of the biopsy punch to cut where necessary without causing excessive movement.
Check regularly during the procedure to prevent cutting too deeply and damaging the meningeal layers or brain tissue.
Extensively rinse the site of the craniotomy with Ringer’s solution.
Cover the exposed brain tissue with Ringer’s solution throughout the surgery.
Remove one CIW from the ethanol and allow it to dry while proceeding with subsequent steps.
Handle the CIWs using blunt forceps to minimize the risk of scratches and damage.
Resuspend DF-1 cells by flicking the Eppendorf tube.
Prepare 2 μL of resuspended DF-1 cells in a Hamilton syringe.
Attach the Hamilton syringe to the stereotactic apparatus.
Position the syringe precisely at the right frontal cortex (2 mm frontal, 1.5 mm lateral from bregma, 2 mm deep).
Inject the cells slowly over a time frame of 10 seconds.
Leave the needle in place for an additional 10 seconds before removing it slowly.
Prepare some Loctite super glue in a Petri dish.
Break a cotton swab in the middle to create a small spatula.
Carefully dry the skull surrounding the craniotomy while leaving Ringer’s solution on top of the brain tissue.
Verify that the CIW is free of any residual ethanol.
Gently place the CIW on the craniotomy hole with the 3-mm diameter coverslip facing the brain.
Apply Loctite super glue at the edges of the 5-mm diameter coverslip using a wooden spatula.
Wait 1–2 min for the glue to dry.
Immerse one side of the head bar into the Loctite super glue and place it on the skull in the lower back corner diagonally opposite to the craniotomy implant window (CIW).
Hold the head bar in place with surgical tweezers until the glue dries.
Mix an equal volume of dental cement powder and solution to prepare a rather fluid dental cement.
Apply the dental cement once it becomes viscous.
Apply dental cement slowly in the empty spaces between skin and skull, starting from the neck area.
Cover the smaller side of the head bar with dental cement.
Seal the space around the CIW without covering it directly.
Use a firmly viscous dental cement to help in sealing.
Make refinements to the dental cement shape using a spatula if needed.
Do not make significant adjustments to prevent detachment of the CIW.
Avoid drilling refinements immediately after application to ensure proper setting.
Remove the mouse from the stereotaxic apparatus once cement is applied.
Turn off the isoflurane anesthesia after removing the mouse.
Weigh the mouse for a baseline measurement.
Place the mouse on a heating pad.
Administer 300 μL of a 0.9% NaCl solution by intraperitoneal injection.
Monitor the mouse until it becomes conscious and then move it back to the housing cage.
Add paracetamol to the mouse’s drinking water for the first 7 days after surgery (500 mg paracetamol per 250 mL water).
Administer 0.9% NaCl daily by intraperitoneal injection until the mouse's weight is equal to or greater than its starting weight.
Wait at least 3 weeks before performing imaging experiments to allow wound healing response triggered by surgery to fully resolve.
Switch on the two-photon microscope before anesthetizing the mouse.
Switch on the climate chamber surrounding the microscope or any other heating system.
Anesthetize the mouse with a 3.5% isoflurane/O2 mixture.
Place the anesthetized mouse on a heating pad with a nose mask to maintain anesthesia at 2% isoflurane/O2 mixture.
Apply eye ointment.
Use a micro-drill to reshape the dental cement around the CIW.
Clean the CIW with acetone until free of glue residues.
Fix the mouse in the head-bar holder under constant isoflurane anesthesia.
Add immersion liquid on top of the CIW depending on the microscope objective.
Completely fill the conical shape of the dental cement to ensure sufficient immersion liquid for the duration of the experiment.
Position the CIW under and perpendicular to the objective.
Screw the head bar to the head-bar holder and place the mouse on the stage of the two-photon microscope with its nose into the anesthesia mask.
Adjust isoflurane levels as necessary, typically around 1%.
Adjust the head-bar holder to ensure that the CIW is positioned perpendicular to the objective.
Depending on the type of objective, add immersion liquid in the dental cement pocket above the CIW to immerse the objective.
Remove the mouse from the microscope after the 2P-IVM session.
Inject approximately 0.5 mL of 0.9% NaCl solution intraperitoneally to rehydrate the mouse.
Return the mouse to its cage and place it on a heating pad.
Visually inspect the mouse until it has fully recovered from anesthesia.
Switch on the MRI machine before anesthetizing the mouse.
Anesthetize the mouse with isoflurane inhalation anesthesia (3.5% isoflurane/O2 mixture).
Apply eye ointment once the mouse is anesthetized.
Transfer the mouse in its natural position to the continuously heated MR cradle and fix the mouse in the tooth bar.
Adjust isoflurane levels to 1.5–2%.
Make sure the mouse’s head is positioned straight before positioning the MRI surface coil.
Insert the cradle into the MR bore, placing the animal’s head at the center of the magnet.
Run a 3-slice localizer to assess the position of the mouse’s head.
Perform initial MR preparation scans suitable for your experimental design.
Tune and match the frequency of the coil to the radiofrequency power.
Compensate for MR field inhomogeneities.
Start the desired protocol on the MRI machine.

Use a 2D turbo rapid acquisition relaxation enhancement (Turbo-RARE) T2-weighted acquisition with TR = 3000 ms, TE = 75 ms, NA = 6, number of slices 10, slice thickness (ST) = 0.7 mm, FOV = 20 × 20 mm², pixel size 0.156 × 0.156 mm², ETL = 12.
Acquire images in axial planes.
Remove the mouse from the cradle after the MRI session.
Return the mouse to its cage.
Visually inspect the mouse until it has fully recovered from anesthesia.
